notes.title: WEGO World War II: Stalingrad | Dev Diary #4
notes.content:
[h3][b]Supply System[/b][/h3][p][/p][p]Supply in [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] is designed to be intuitive and low-maintenance - handled mostly by exception. If you’re on the defensive, you can largely ignore it. But when going on the offensive or planning large maneuvers, you’ll need to engage with it directly and strategically.[/p][p]At the start of each turn, all HQs reset to [b]Basic Supply[/b]. You can change supply to [b]Move+[/b], [b]Combat+[/b], or both, giving subordinate units more fuel (for extended movement) or ammo (for higher combat effectiveness). But this comes at a cost - if a unit is given [b]Combat+ [/b]supply but does not use it, that supply is lost, so poor planning wastes resources.[/p][p]Supply flows from [b]Main Supply Sources[/b], down through the HQ chain, via [b]Lines of Communication (LOC)[/b]. Units out of range are penalized, and supply effectiveness degrades if interdicted.[/p][list][*][p][b]Combat+[/b] boosts attack performance.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Move+[/b] enables road movement and extended operations.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Interdiction[/b] from enemy air/naval assets can disrupt delivery, but can be countered by friendly Counter-Air missions.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Supply Depots[/b] and [b]Airfields[/b] can keep isolated forces going, albeit at reduced effectiveness.[/p][/*][/list][p]Whether you're pushing through open terrain or clinging to a battered city block, smart supply management is vital to keeping your forces in fighting shape.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45637059/2af995edc5869132cec37f6cd3aa7451a0059b24.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][h3][b]Lines of Communication (LOC)[/b][/h3][p][/p][p]In [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b], maintaining your [b]Lines of Communication (LOC)[/b] is essential for keeping your units supplied and effective in combat. Every HQ and ground unit falls into one of four LOC states based on distance (in movement points) and whether a clear path exists back to supply:[/p][list][*][p][b]Supported[/b] – Fully in supply, with access to supply types ([b]Combat+[/b], [b]Move+[/b]). Only supported units can use Road Movement.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Extended Support[/b] – Still supplied, but too far for road movement. All supply types can be assigned, but mobility is reduced, and their readiness recovery rate is reduced.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Isolated[/b] – Out of range from any HQ. Shock effects are halved, and supply options are severely limited.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Encircled[/b] – Surrounded with no supply path at all. These units suffer halved shock effects and lose readiness every turn.[/p][/*][/list][p]Managing LOCs—especially in fluid battles or deep advances—is key. Let your front outrun your supply lines, and your offensive may grind to a halt.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]Shock Mechanics[/b][/h3][p][/p][h3]Shock in [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] represents the impact of high-mobility, high-intensity combat from armored and mechanized units. It shifts the odds in combat, simulating the advantage of speed, force, and surprise in open terrain.[/h3][list][*][p][b]Armored units[/b] always have a [b]Shock value of 4[/b], regardless of tank model.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Foot infantry[/b] reduce Shock effectiveness by slowing down the overall attack—tanks have to match their pace.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Mechanized infantry[/b] and [b]motorized units[/b] do not have shock but they don’t reduce it.[/p][/*][*][p]Shock is only applied in [b]open terrain[/b], and not when attacking across rough hexsides like gullies.

[/p][/*][/list][h3]Shock effectiveness is calculated by:[/h3][olist][*][p]Taking the [b]highest Shock value[/b] among attacking units.[/p][/*][*][p]Adjusting it based on the proportion of “Shock-capable” stacking size (i.e. units with Shock vs. total stacking).[/p][/*][*][p]Halving Shock if units are understrength, low on readiness, or isolated/encircled. Units in extremely poor condition contribute no Shock.
[/p][/*][/olist][h3][b]Example[/b]: If a Shock 4 tank unit is attacking alongside infantry, and half the stacking comes from non-Shock units, then only half of the Shock is used - yielding a final Shock of 2. This can significantly alter the combat odds.[/h3][h3][b]Anti-Tank Units[/b]:[/h3][list][*][p]Standard AT guns [b]neutralize up to 2 points of enemy Shock[/b] but don’t contribute to offensive Shock.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Heavy German AT/AA units[/b] (e.g. 88mm) can attack with [b]Shock 2[/b], but only against tanks and under specific conditions (e.g. longer range, supporting other AT units).[/p][/*][/list][h3]Shock adds an extra layer of tactical planning—grouping fast units together maximizes their impact, while mixing them with slower infantry can blunt their edge.[/h3][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45637059/e41e610181d9de5551c77a0ef7ed58d0307e82f5.png"][/img][/p][h3][b]Battle Types[/b][/h3][p][/p][p][b]Planned Attacks[/b][/p][p]These are the cornerstone of your offensive strategy. When your units are adjacent to the enemy, you can launch a [b]Planned Attack[/b] — a coordinated assault backed by [b]Artillery[/b], [b]Air Support[/b], and [b]Command Support[/b] to tilt the odds in your favor.[/p][p]You’ll see the expected combat odds before committing (or an estimate, if [b]Fog of War[/b] is enabled), allowing you to make informed, strategic decisions. To launch a Planned Attack, simply move your units onto the target hex — the rest is in your hands.[/p][p][b]Ad-hoc Attacks[/b][/p][p]Not every battle is planned in advance. [b]Ad-hoc Attacks[/b] happen dynamically during movement — when a moving unit encounters enemy forces on the way to its destination. These engagements are [b]unplanned[/b] and inherently more chaotic.[/p][p]Because both sides may be moving simultaneously, you can never be entirely sure how the battle will unfold. The enemy might withdraw, reinforce, or shift positions, while your own units might be delayed by Command & Control penalties. In these situations, your units won’t have access to offensive support — but stationary defenders will benefit from their assigned artillery, air, or command bonuses.[/p][h3][b]Types of Ad-hoc Engagements[/b][/h3][list][*][p][b]Meeting Engagements
[/b] When both sides move into the same area, chaos reigns. [b]No terrain advantages[/b] apply, but [b]unit quality [/b]becomes critical — higher-quality troops perform better in these unpredictable skirmishes, with their [b]quality bonus doubled[/b] in the fight.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Ambushes
[/b] If your units are using [b]Road Movement[/b] and end up adjacent to an enemy, they’ll be caught in an ambush. Movement stops immediately, and the enemy strikes first — with no return fire from your side. Fast, risky, and potentially devastating.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Overruns
[/b] Got overwhelming force? If your units reach a [b]10:1 odds ratio[/b] during movement, they can [b]overrun[/b] the enemy — wiping out the defenders and continuing their advance in a single, crushing blow. It’s rare, but when it happens, it’s spectacular.[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][h3][b]Combine & Breakdown — Unit Flexibility Without the Clutter[/b][/h3][p]In some games, excessive stacking made dense areas difficult to manage. For [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b], we wanted to capture both tactical depth and clean battlefield visibility, especially at a scale of 2.5 km per hex.[/p][p]The solution? Flexible unit representation.[/p][p]You can switch between [b]Regiments/Brigades[/b] represented by a single counter, or break them down into three Battalion-level units for finer control where it matters. This allows you to:[/p][list][*][p]Cover broad fronts with battalions when space is tight[/p][/*][*][p]Consolidate into regiments to reduce clutter and streamline command[/p][/*][*][p]Seamlessly switch between the two as the tactical situation demands[/p][/*][*][p][/p][/*][/list][p]This system gives you the flexibility to scale your force structure without sacrificing clarity or control.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]Command and Control — Leadership Matters[/b][/h3][p]Units in [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] don’t just follow orders instantly. They operate within a realistic [b]Command & Control system[/b], where timing, coordination, and leadership quality matter.[/p][list][*][p]Orders may be delayed depending on a unit’s distance from HQ and its command rating.[/p][/*][*][p]Better commanders and shorter communication lines mean faster, more reliable execution.[/p][/*][*][p]Units may hesitate, arrive late, or even misinterpret commands under pressure.
[/p][/*][/list][p]This adds an extra layer of realism — planning isn’t just about what to do, but [b]when and how effectively[/b] it will happen.[/p][p][/p][p]Out on [b]June 25th:[/b][/p][p][dynamiclink href="https://store.steampowered.com/app/3547040/WEGO_World_War_II_Stalingrad/"][/dynamiclink][/p][p]
[/p]

notes.title: WEGO World War II: Stalingrad | Dev Diary #3
notes.content: [h3][b]Fog of War[/b][/h3][p]The Fog of War in [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] keeps tension high and certainty low. Your intel is never complete, and enemy movements—hidden or misjudged—can upend even the best-laid plans. Units have limited [b]Intel Range[/b] and [b]Intel Strength[/b], so smart commanders must scout proactively using [b]Recce units[/b], [b]Air Recon[/b], and assets like [b]radio intercepts[/b].[/p][p]Unlike in many wargames, Recce units here aren’t just weak infantry—they’re essential tools. With superior recon capabilities and the ability to [b]automatically withdraw[/b] from enemy contact (unless ordered to hold), they’re built to survive and report - not be sacrificed. No more losing nimble scouts to plodding foot soldiers.[/p][p]Fail to scout properly, and you may find your forces walking blind into disaster.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45637059/6da85ecf97db110327751d983bfb75cb696aecf9.png"][/img][/p][h3][b]Off-Map Assets[/b][/h3][p]In [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b], the action isn’t confined to the map. [b]Off-map assets[/b] play a crucial role in shaping the battlefield. You’ll have access to a wide range of support options, including [b]airstrikes, naval bombardments, command support, intelligence operations[/b], and even [b]partisans[/b] or [b]special forces[/b] units. These assets offer strategic depth without cluttering the map, giving you the flexibility to influence the battle from afar, [b]interdict [/b]enemy logistics, protect your forces from enemy air strikes via [b]counter-air[/b], or provide critical reinforcement when your forces need it most.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]Game Editor[/b][/h3][p]For those looking to create, [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] includes a [b]complete game editor[/b], opening the door to endless customization. Modders can create custom maps, units, scenarios, campaigns, and even AI scripts to bring their own visions of war to life. This extensive toolset not only extends the game’s longevity but allows players to continually evolve and expand the game's content. Whether you're a seasoned modder who wants to create an entirely new scenario, or someone who just wants to tweak a few aspects of gameplay, the editor offers limitless possibilities.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]Tactical and Operational Balance[/b][/h3][p]The game’s [b]dual ground scales[/b] and [b]time scales[/b] strike the perfect balance between operational strategy and tactical combat. On the operational maps, set at a[b] 2.5 km scale[/b], you’ll maneuver large formations and plan broad strategic offensives over the Russian steppes. For the urban combat of Stalingrad, the [b]500-meter tactical maps[/b] provide a more granular focus on street-to-street fighting. With five turns per day on operational maps and two turns per day on tactical maps, the game lets you experience both the grand scale of battle and the chaos of city warfare. This balance ensures you’re never just playing for the next move — you're managing an entire campaign while still engaging in intense, close-quarters combat.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]Challenging AI and Multiplayer Options[/b][/h3][p]The [b]AI[/b] in [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] offers a formidable challenge, particularly for solo players who will face an opponent that is both strategically smart and unpredictable. But the real excitement comes when you go head-to-head with a human opponent. With [b]hotseat[/b] and [b]Play By Email (PBEM)[/b] multiplayer modes, you can engage in tense, slow-burn battles or rapid-fire confrontations. The WEGO system’s unpredictability ensures that both the AI and human opponents are always engaging, as you’ll never know exactly how your opponent will react, forcing you to think on your feet and adapt your strategy at every turn.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]AI Assist[/b][/h3][p]To keep gameplay smooth and focused on big-picture strategy, [b]WEGO WWII: Stalingrad[/b] includes powerful AI Assist tools that can handle routine tasks at your command. Speed up your turns and focus on what matters most.[/p][p]At any point during your turn — or automatically at turn start — you can have the AI:[/p][list][*][p][b]Assign Ground Attacks[/b][/p][/*][*][p][b]Assign Artillery Strikes[/b][/p][/*][*][p][b]Allocate Air and Ground Support Assets [/b][/p][/*][/list][p]Plus, you can now [b]move entire organizations[/b] with a single order. Just give a destination to one unit, and the rest of its formation will follow — making large-scale maneuvers faster and more intuitive.[/p][p][/p][h3][b]Out on June 25th[/b][/h3][p][dynamiclink href="https://store.steampowered.com/app/3547040/WEGO_World_War_II_Stalingrad/"][/dynamiclink][/p]

notes.title: WEGO World War II: Stalingrad | Dev Diary #2
notes.content:
[h2][b]Why WEGO?[/b][/h2]

WEGO WWII: Stalingrad breaks away from traditional turn-based systems by using a WEGO (We Go) system, where both players plan their moves simultaneously. The result? A dynamic and unpredictable battle where you have to anticipate your opponent’s actions and react to shifting circumstances — all without knowing exactly what they’ll do next and with fog of war, without even knowing the location or exact strength of their reserves. This system introduces a level of uncertainty (and tactical opportunities!) that are not present in normal turn-based games, forcing players to try and manage the chaos in every turn.

[b]Why Stalingrad?[/b]
WEGO WWII: Stalingrad covers the German 1942 campaign from Operation Heron in July through to the ferocious urban fighting in November. This was one of the most pivotal and brutal confrontations of World War II—a battle that began with the German 6th Army’s rapid advance across the southern steppes and ended in a desperate, close-quarters struggle amid the ruins of Stalingrad itself.

The game spans this transformation, offering scenarios that range from mobile operations in open terrain to intense street fighting inside the city. Each scenario is built around carefully researched Orders of Battle, on both land and in the air, delivering historical authenticity while giving players the opportunity to rewrite – or relive – critical moments of the campaign.

Stalingrad’s unique mix of tactical complexity and operational scale makes it the perfect setting for a WEGO wargame – challenging players to adapt to shifting conditions, manage chaos, and make hard choices under pressure.
